data.sourcePassage:
In 1707, the Act of Union joined the Kingdom of England (including Wales) and the Kingdom of Scotland into a new state: the Kingdom of Great Britain. A single Parliament met at Westminster. Scotland lost its separate Parliament but kept its own legal system and its Presbyterian church.

The Act of Union did not happen because everyone agreed it was a good idea. It resulted from a combination of political pressures, economic problems and strategic calculations.

England feared that Scotland might choose a different Protestant successor after Queen Anne died without surviving children, which could break the shared monarchy created in 1603. England also worried that Scotland might ally with France against it. The Alien Act of 1705 put economic pressure on Scotland by threatening to treat Scots as aliens and restrict their trade with England.

Scotland had its own reasons for considering union. The failure of the Darien Scheme in the 1690s had left many Scottish investors bankrupt and weakened the country economically. Union offered access to English colonial trade and a financial payment called the Equivalent to compensate for Darien losses.

Opposition was strong in Scotland. Many people feared the loss of the Scottish Parliament, higher taxes, and domination by English interests. There were protests in Edinburgh. However, the Act was passed in both Parliaments in 1706 and 1707 and came into effect on 1 May 1707. Ireland was not part of this union — it remained a separate kingdom under British control until 1801.

questions.question: What new state was created by the Act of Union in 1707?
options: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
The Kingdom of Great Britain
The British Empire
The Commonwealth of Nations
questions.modelAnswer: The Act of Union created the Kingdom of Great Britain, formed from England (including Wales) and Scotland, with a single Parliament at Westminster.

questions.question: How did the Alien Act of 1705 put pressure on Scotland to accept union?
options: By invading Scotland with English troops
By threatening to treat Scots as aliens and restrict their trade with England
By refusing to pay Scotland's debts from the Darien Scheme
By choosing a different Scottish Parliament
questions.modelAnswer: The Alien Act threatened to treat Scottish people as aliens and restrict their trade with England unless Scotland accepted negotiations about succession and union.

questions.question: What economic problem made some Scots more willing to consider union?
options: Scotland had too much gold and needed somewhere to trade it
The failure of the Darien Scheme left many Scottish investors bankrupt
Scottish factories were producing too many goods for the domestic market
Scotland owed England large amounts of tax money
questions.modelAnswer: The failure of the Darien colonial scheme in Panama in the 1690s had left many Scottish investors bankrupt and weakened the country economically, making access to English trade attractive.

questions.question: Why is it inaccurate to say the United Kingdom was created in 1707?
options: Because the Act of Union was not passed until 1714
Because Ireland was not part of the 1707 union and only joined in 1801
Because Wales had its own Parliament until 1800
Because England refused to allow Scotland to join until 1714
questions.modelAnswer: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland was only created in 1801 when Ireland joined. The 1707 Act created the Kingdom of Great Britain, which did not include Ireland.

data.sourcePassage:
Jacobites supported the Stuart dynasty's claim to the British throne. After James II and VII was removed in the Glorious Revolution of 1688, his descendants became the focus of Jacobite hopes. When Queen Anne died in 1714 without surviving children, Parliament had the Protestant George I of Hanover inherit the throne. Many Jacobites were furious.

Jacobitism was not simple. Different people supported it for different reasons. Some believed in hereditary monarchy and that the Stuarts had a rightful claim. Some Scottish opponents of the Act of Union saw Jacobitism as a way to reverse 1707. Some Highland clans supported the Stuarts because of local loyalties. Some Catholics hoped for better treatment. English Tories who disliked Hanoverian rule were also sometimes sympathetic.

The first major Jacobite rising came in 1715, led by the Earl of Mar in Scotland. It lacked coordination and clear strategy, received limited English support, and failed after a government victory at Preston in England and an inconclusive battle at Sheriffmuir in Scotland. James Francis Edward Stuart, the Old Pretender, arrived too late to turn the situation around.

The 1745 rising was more dramatic. Charles Edward Stuart landed in the Hebrides with a small group of supporters. He raised support in the Highlands, captured Edinburgh and won the Battle of Prestonpans in September 1745. The Jacobite army marched south and reached Derby in December 1745 — the furthest they had ever penetrated into England. However, the Jacobite leaders were uncertain about English support and French invasion plans. They chose to retreat to Scotland. This decision damaged morale. Though the Jacobites won at Falkirk Muir in January 1746, they were finally defeated at the Battle of Culloden on 16 April 1746.

questions.question: What was the furthest south the Jacobite army reached in 1745?
options: London
Derby
York
Edinburgh
questions.modelAnswer: The Jacobite army reached Derby in December 1745, which was the furthest south they ever penetrated into England before retreating.

questions.question: According to the passage, why did the Jacobites retreat from Derby?
options: They had run out of food and supplies
Charles Edward Stuart was injured at Derby
Their leaders were uncertain about English support and French invasion plans
The government army had surrounded them at Derby
questions.modelAnswer: The Jacobite leaders chose to retreat from Derby because they were uncertain about the level of English support they would receive and about whether France would invade to help them.

questions.question: Why was Jacobitism supported by different groups for different reasons?
options: All Jacobites wanted exactly the same outcome: a Catholic Stuart king
Some wanted to restore the Stuarts, some to reverse union, some for religious reasons, some for local clan loyalties
Jacobitism was only a Scottish movement with no English supporters
All Highlanders were Jacobites because they hated the English
questions.modelAnswer: Jacobitism attracted support for many different reasons: some believed in hereditary monarchy, some opposed the Act of Union, some were Catholic, some were Highland clan leaders, and some English Tories disliked Hanoverian rule.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about the reason the 1715 rising failed?
options: The Jacobites were too well organised and frightened the government
It lacked coordination, strategy and broad English support, and James arrived too late
It was betrayed by Charles Edward Stuart
George I personally led the army against the Jacobites
questions.modelAnswer: The 1715 rising failed because it lacked coordination and clear strategy, received limited English support, and James Francis Edward Stuart, the Old Pretender, arrived too late to help.

data.sourceTitle: The Battle of Culloden and Its Aftermath
data.targetTitle: The Battle of Culloden and Its Aftermath
data.sourcePassage:
The Battle of Culloden on 16 April 1746 was the final defeat of the Jacobite cause. The Duke of Cumberland's government forces, better equipped and supplied, overwhelmed the Jacobite army in less than an hour on wet moorland near Inverness. Charles Edward Stuart fled and eventually escaped to France, where he lived in exile until his death in 1788.

The British government responded to the Jacobite threat with systematic measures designed to prevent any future rising. Many Jacobite leaders were executed, imprisoned or forced into exile. Some rebel landowners had their estates confiscated. The government built new military roads and forts across the Highlands to improve communication and control.

Laws directly targeted the power of Highland clans. The Heritable Jurisdictions Act of 1746 reduced the traditional legal powers of clan chiefs over their people. The Disarming Acts restricted the possession of weapons. The Dress Act made it illegal for many people to wear Highland dress including tartan.

These measures changed Highland society, but they did not destroy Highland culture completely. Gaelic language, music and memory survived. Over time, the Highlands were transformed not only by government policy but also by economic pressure, landlord decisions and wider social change.

After Culloden, British identity gradually became more established. Some Scots embraced Britishness because of opportunities through trade, empire, military service and government. Identity in Britain was not simple: people could feel Scottish and British, Welsh and British, or hold several identities at once. The old Jacobite cause lost its practical military force, though memories and mythology surrounding figures like Bonnie Prince Charlie persisted in song and story.

questions.question: Where did Charles Edward Stuart go after Culloden?
options: He was captured and imprisoned in Edinburgh
He fled and eventually escaped to France, living there in exile
He surrendered to the Duke of Cumberland immediately
He returned to the Highlands and continued fighting
questions.modelAnswer: After Culloden, Charles Edward Stuart fled and eventually escaped to France, where he lived in exile until his death in 1788.

questions.question: What was the purpose of the Heritable Jurisdictions Act of 1746?
options: To give clan chiefs more power over their people
To reduce the traditional legal powers of Highland clan chiefs
To create new courts for Jacobite trials
To protect Highland dress and cultural traditions
questions.modelAnswer: The Heritable Jurisdictions Act reduced the traditional legal powers of Highland clan chiefs over their people, weakening their authority and reducing the likelihood of future clan-based rebellion.

questions.question: According to the passage, what did the Dress Act restrict?
options: The right of Lowland Scots to wear English-style clothing
Many people from wearing Highland dress including tartan
The wearing of military uniforms by government soldiers
The display of Jacobite symbols in churches
questions.modelAnswer: The Dress Act made it illegal for many people to wear Highland dress including tartan, as part of the government's effort to suppress Jacobite culture and Highland identity.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about identity after Culloden?
options: Culloden forced everyone to give up Scottish identity and become only British
People could hold multiple identities such as Scottish and British at the same time
All Scots rejected Britishness after the harsh treatment following Culloden
Identity in Britain became fixed and simple after 1746
questions.modelAnswer: The passage shows that identity was not simple after Culloden: people could feel both Scottish and British, Welsh and British, or hold several identities, and some Scots embraced British identity for practical reasons such as trade and empire.
